**Where we are ahead:** the request path is built in — body, typed body, query, typed query and path-param middleware answering an aggregated 400 (or RFC 9457 problem details from the core), which the struct validators leave to the framework; **JSON DoS caps** (depth, array size, members, nodes) enforced by a token scan before the tree exists; a streaming path that validates and decodes in one tokenization into a fixed per-request buffer (~1.5x the body); JSON Schema **export** (`writeJsonSchema`, `writeJsonSchemaFor`); pydantic-style one-error-per-wrong-type aggregation. **Where we are behind:** `pattern` has no built-in regex (the repo's `regex` module exists, `validate` does not depend on it yet, see Backlog -- a caller-supplied `Pattern.matcher` covers it); the go-playground tag count (~170) is matched for the pure string formats (96 formats since 2026-11-19, `html` the last: 95 since 2026-11-05, the second wave added colours, ISBN/ISSN, crypto addresses, `fqdn`, `dns_rfc1035_label`, `datauri`, URNs, socket-address syntax, ISO 3166-1/4217 code sets, BCP 47 syntax, BIC, card/Luhn, `cve`, `ssn`, `ein`, `cron`); still missing: `iso3166_2` (a 1,000-entry table, generated the same way as the others), `postcode_iso3166_alpha2*` (a regex per country), `timezone` (needs the tz database; the `tz` module has it), `latitude`/`longitude`, `boolean`, `json`, `port` (integer kinds), `alphaspace`, hash-digest hex lengths (`md5`, `sha256`, ...), `printascii`, `number`; `non_control_character` has no go-playground tag (its Keats/validator semantics, vectors in `formats_extra_test.zig`); the `*_addr` formats are syntax only; no `eqcsfield`-style cross-STRUCT paths (a cross rule names a sibling in the same object), no `isdefault`, `fieldcontains`/`fieldexcludes`, rules for the keys or values of an object with open keys (`dive`, `keys`, `endkeys`), a validate-only-these-fields entry point (`StructPartial`), tag-string parsing (rules are Zig values), custom type functions or translations; cross-field comparisons treat arrays and objects as never equal (go compares lengths); bounds are f64 (an integer value is held to one exactly since 2026-10-24, and integers compare exactly in cross-field comparisons, past i64 too).

## Design & invariants
Three tiers: a pure `Rule`-set validator core (no HTTP) → the typed style `parseInto(T, gpa, body)`
(comptime-reflected schema from struct `T`: optionals → nullable, defaults → not-required, int
bit-width → bounds, enums → `one_of`) plus a runtime-schema style `validateJson`/`validateValue` over
`std.json.Value` → `Body`/`TypedBody(T)`/`Query`/`PathParams` middleware for `router`. Never
fail-fast: every failure is aggregated into the `Report`; a wrong-typed field gets exactly one
`<kind>_type` error (no constraint noise) and other fields keep reporting (pydantic behavior). JSON
DoS caps (`Limits`): a fail-fast streaming token scan (`std.json.Scanner`) enforces `max_depth` (32),
`max_array_elements` (10,000), `max_object_members` (1,000) and `max_total_nodes` (1,000,000) *before*
the document is materialized into a `std.json.Value` tree — a cheap-to-send, expensive-to-parse
payload (deep nesting, huge arrays/objects) is rejected before it can blow up memory/CPU; a breach
yields a clean `too_deep`/`array_too_large`/`too_many_fields`/`too_many_nodes` error, never a panic or
an OOM. Allocation: one arena per validation run, owned by the returned `Report` (`deinit` frees
everything); codes are static strings, composed paths/messages live in the arena, simple paths borrow
`Rule.field` — the schema must outlive the Report. Middleware state is immutable after init, shared
across connection threads (reentrant); success data flows to handlers via a magic-tagged, stackable
`ctx.data` slot chain (`Query` + `Body` compose on one route). Format validators are pure: no
allocation, never panic on any byte sequence. Clean-room; design references pydantic v2 (error shape
+ code vocabulary), JSON Schema draft 2020-12 (keyword semantics + format vocabulary), and
go-playground/validator (struct-tag ergonomics) — behavior/format only, no source copied — see NOTICE.

**Typed query** (`parseQueryLeaky`): a query string decoded into struct `T`
under `rulesFor(T)` + `T.validate_rules` (a `pub` decl: Zig 0.17 `@hasDecl` ignores private ones), with `validateQuery`'s decoding and coercion (lenient
percent-decoding, first duplicate wins, unknown keys ignored). Fields are what one query value can
spell (bool, ints, floats, enums, `[]const u8`, `[N]u8`, `?U` of those; else a compile error); a
field is optional when it has a default. One walk over the query, keys compared as they decode
(no allocation per key); strings borrowed from the query when they needed no decoding.

**Streaming path** (`parseIntoLeaky`, `validateJsonStreaming`): the same rules without
the `std.json.Value` tree, for servers that decode into a fixed per-request buffer. The tree is 30–60×
the body (FBA minimum for `parseIntoLimited`: 16.5 KiB body → 955 KiB); the streaming path needs
~1.5× the body + ~2 KiB (same body → 25 KiB). One pass over `std.json.Scanner` tokens: a scalar
becomes a one-node `Value` and goes through the SAME `checkRule` (one implementation of the type gate,
constraints and messages); containers are walked in place (`required` settled at object end,
`min_len`/`max_len` at array end); a container whose rule has `custom` is materialized — that subtree
only — and checked by the tree code; error paths are stack-frame chains rendered only when an error
is recorded; both typed rule sets (derived + `T.validate_rules`) are walked together and
deduplicated as in the tree path. The walker is push-shaped (an explicit frame stack, fed one whole
token at a time), so for a typed body `std.json.parseFromTokenSourceLeaky(T)` pulls the tokens
through a tap that feeds each to the walker, which checks the structural limits on the way too:
**one tokenization** (the limit check, the walk and the decode share it; `parseOnePass`). A document the
decoder refuses, or the walker stops (duplicate key, a limit), is answered by the multi-pass path
instead (`parseMultiPass`: pre-scan, walk, `parseFromSliceLeaky`) -- so an invalid document gets exactly the report
and precedence it always had. Strings are borrowed from the body. Differences by design: errors in document order (tree: schema order), and a
different subset past `max_errors`. Equality of the error SET and of decoded values is pinned by a
differential fuzz target against the tree path.

**Compiled typed path** (`parseCompiled`): in front of `parseOnePass`, for every `T`
whose shape and rules allow it (`compiles`: scalars, structs, slices, optionals of them; no `cross`
rule, no `custom` on a container, every rule naming a member `T` has). The walker interprets —
each token goes through `Walker.feed`, keys are matched against both rule sets at run time,
`checkRule` reads rules as data. For a typed body all of that is known at compile time, so this is
a decoder generated from `T` and both rule sets: it drives the scanner itself, decodes every
scalar with std's own `innerParse` (through a one-token source, so values are std's by
construction), and at each value runs exactly the walker's checks in the walker's order, with
`checkRule` inlined on a comptime rule. Reporting is the walker's (`use`, `path`, `gate`,
`finish`), so errors, their order, the cap and the second set's deduplication are the same. It
answers only what it can answer exactly as `parseOnePass` would; a syntax or decode error, a
limit, a duplicate key at any depth, an escaped key (also inside a skipped member),
trailing data, or a value of a shape the type cannot hold makes it give up, and the old paths
answer. The `compiled` fuzz harness requires the identical answer — equal values, or the same
errors in the same order — on every document it answers (`expectCompiledAgrees`).
Speed: `zig build bench-validate`, see Performance.

**Cross-field rules** (`Rule.cross`; parity -- go-playground `eqfield`, `nefield`, `gtfield`,
`gtefield`, `ltfield`, `ltefield`, `required_if`, `required_unless`, `required_with`, `required_without`,
baked_in.go 1372, 1042, 2343, 2299, 2571, 2527, 2120, 2160, 2219, 2264). One implementation (`checkCross`)
for both paths: the tree hands it the object's members, the streaming `Walker` the scalars it captured while
the object went by (`Frame.caps`: only the members some rule's `cross` names, strings copied because the
token is freed after `feed`; a container is recorded as such), and it runs when the object is complete, beside
`required`. Names: codes `field_mismatch` (eq), `field_equal` (ne), `greater_than_field`,
`greater_than_equal_field`, `less_than_field`, `less_than_equal_field`; the presence ops report `missing`.
"Present" is key presence (an explicit `null` is present, as for `required`); go tests the Go zero value, which
JSON cannot tell from absence -- the one named semantic difference. Comparison ops skip a null and a field that
failed its own type gate (one error per field, no noise); a missing sibling fails `eq` and the orderings and
passes `ne` (go: `!ok`). Numbers compare by value (two integers exactly), two date-times / two dates
chronologically (go compares `time.Time`), other strings for `eq` by text and for the orderings by byte length
(go compares `len`). `required_if` needs every entry, `required_unless` any exemption, `required_with` any
present sibling, `required_without` any absent one -- go's own quantifiers. The later presence ops: `required_with_all` / `required_without_all` need every named sibling present / absent, `skip_unless` is `required_if` (baked_in.go `skipUnless` has `requiredIf`'s body in v10.30.5 although its comment copies `requiredUnless`'s), and the `excluded_*` family runs on a PRESENT field (an explicit `null` or a wrong-typed value counts, the key is there) and answers `excluded`: `excluded_if` when every entry holds, `excluded_unless` when none does, `excluded_with` / `excluded_without` when any sibling is present / absent, `excluded_with_all` / `excluded_without_all` when every one is. `excluded_without` reads ONE name per entry, as go's function does: several entries are several go tags, each judged alone, so "any"; go's `excluded_without=A B` is the single name "A B", never found, so the field is always refused, and an `other` of `"A B"` here is the same literal key. `tools/cross_oracle.py` replays all of them against go-playground (`go_cross_test.zig`). A `custom` predicate on a container
materializes that subtree and the tree code (same `checkCross`) decides inside it. Not exported to JSON Schema:
the comparison ops (2020-12 cannot compare two members); `required_with` is `dependentRequired`, the other
presence ops `allOf` items.

On query and path params (`validateQuery`, `validateParams`, so the `Query` and `PathParams` middlewares) `Rule.cross` runs over the coerced values (`CrossSlots`, one `checkCross` for every path). Every schema rule is a slot, coerced as its own kind (`int` by value, so `9` < `10`); a sibling named only by a `cross` entry is read and coerced as the kind of the rule that names it. Not sent is absent (the presence ops see it; a missing sibling fails `eq` and the orderings and passes `ne`); sent but not coercible is present and incomparable (it keeps its own `int_parsing`-style error, gets no comparison noise, and still counts as present for `required_with` / `required_without`). `Rule.code` / `message` overrides apply as in a body. `parseQueryLeaky`'s `validate_rules` ignores `cross` (see Backlog).

**Unique and numeric `one_of`.** `Rule.unique` (JSON Schema `uniqueItems`, go-playground `unique`): an array's items must be pairwise distinct under JSON equality (`1` = `1.0`; objects by members whatever their order; integers past i64 compare exactly as digits, `numberOrder`). `firstDuplicate` finds the first pair in O(n log n): items are sorted by a 128-bit SipHash structural hash and only neighbours with equal hashes are compared, so an array of `max_array_elements` items is no DoS lever. The streaming paths materialize the array. `one_of` on an `.int` / `.float` rule compares the entries' number texts to the value by value (go-playground `oneof=5 7 9`).

**Typed integers.** A float-spelled integer (`1e3`, `1.0`) is taken for an integer field only when it is integral and inside the type, with an EXCLUSIVE upper end at the exact power of two (`floatFitsInt`: 2^63 and 2^64 for `i64` / `u64` would be a safety panic in std's decoder); a 128-bit member takes float-spelled values only below 2^127, on both entry points (`parseIntoLeaky` decodes such a `T` through the checked `Value` route). Integer-spelled values and the derived rules are unchanged, so the JSON Schema export does not move.

**Format profile.** `uri` and `uri_reference` follow RFC 3986 §3.2.3 for the port (`port = *DIGIT`, as Go's `net/url`: `http://host:abc/` is no URI; `uriPortOk`), take `[` / `]` only in an IP-literal host, and `origin` refuses an unbracketed IPv6 literal (a `:` in the host after the port split, `http://::1:80`). `lowercase` / `uppercase` match go exactly: their change-sets come from Go's `unicode` package (`isCased` is ASCII + Latin-1, `tools/go_casetables`). `html` is go's `<[/]?([a-zA-Z]+).*?>` (`isHtml`: linear per line).

**Rule vocabulary** (parity with go-playground's parameterized tags and Rust validator's `code`/`message`). `gt`/`lt`, `none_of`, `ignore_case`, `patterns`, the `Pattern` shapes `contains`, `contains_any`, `excludes`, `excludes_any`, `not_prefix`, `not_suffix`, `omit_empty`, `omit_zero`, `any_of`, `code`, `message`, and `Error.param`. All scalar checks live in `checkRuleBody`, which every path reaches, so one implementation serves tree, walker and compiled path. What a path does outside it, `Rule.code`/`message` reach through `overrideSince` (missing, array bounds at the container's end, the container type gate, cross-field). A container with `any_of` or `omit_zero` needs its whole value, so it is materialized as for `custom` and `unique` (`needsWholeContainer`), and the compiled path declines it.

- **`omit_empty`, decided against go.** Go's `omitempty` is about Go values: `null` decodes to a nil pointer or a zero value, a non-nil empty slice has a value. So: `null`, `""`, `0`, `false` skip, `[]` and `{}` do not (`omit_zero` takes them, as `hasNotZeroValue` does), and the value must fit the kind (`0` on a string rule still fails its type gate). `required` stays key presence and `cross` still runs. On a query or path value the empty text is empty for every kind, so `?age=` passes an int rule where it would be `int_parsing`.
- **`ignore_case`** folds with Go's `unicode.SimpleFold` orbits (`case_tables.zig`, `fold_to_canonical`, generated by `tools/go_casetables`), so U+212A folds to `k` and `ß` does not equal `ss`, as `strings.EqualFold`.
- **`any_of`** gives one error whatever the alternatives said, go's and pydantic's `union` shape differ here and go's is the one with a stable code. An alternative runs on a scratch builder capped at one error. Caps, both fail closed: 64 nested alternatives (twice the default `max_depth`; a caller who raises that gets the error on a recursive shape deeper than this), and `Limits.max_any_of_steps`, by default 2^22 rule evaluations inside alternatives in one validation. The budget counts work, not alternatives: about 12 evaluations per node of a 1 MiB body, and 400,000 scalars under three alternatives is a test. Without it a rule graph looping through `any_of` overflows the stack, and a benign recursive schema with two alternatives takes 2^depth on a crafted document, inside the default limits. Inside an alternative the walk stops at the first error.
- **`omit_zero` on the streaming paths materializes the container,** as `custom` and `unique` do, and costs their memory.
- **`Error.actual_code`** (go's `ActualTag`) is the built-in code when an override touched the error. `dedupeFrom` compares it, so `Rule.code` does not make one failure two, and the caller's override replaces the derived rule's entry.

- **Export:** every one has a 2020-12 form except `ignore_case`, which goes out as an annotation (looser, never stricter, class `IGNORE_CASE`), and `code`/`message`, which mean nothing to a schema. A negated pattern is `not` + `type: string` + `pattern`, because `not` of a bare `pattern` refuses every non-string. A pattern whose regex text is longer than `writeRegex`'s buffer (`regex_buf_len`, 512 bytes) exports as `.*` when positive and says nothing when negated (`.*` under `not` would refuse everything). A `literal` (`const` / `enum`) is stated only on `.string` and `.any` rules, and `one_of` / `none_of` only there and on `.int` / `.float` (where they are numeric): a `.bool` / `.array` / `.object` rule says nothing for them, as the module ignores them there; non-literal patterns stay (`pattern` over non-strings is vacuous).

**Shared sub-rules in the export.** `writeJsonSchema*` scans the rule graph first (identity of `*const Rule`: the same `items` pointer, `fields` or `any_of` slice element) and writes every rule that has children and is reached by more than one edge ONCE under `"$defs"` of the root object as `"rule<N>"` (N in order of first discovery); each place that reaches it holds `{"$ref":"#/$defs/rule<N>"}`. A loop (`.items = &self`) becomes a `$ref` to its own definition, so it is exported exactly instead of cut at `max_schema_nesting` (240) levels. Leaves (no `items`/`fields`/`any_of`) stay inline. Reference: JSON Schema 2020-12 sections 8.2.4 (`$defs`) and 8.2.3.1 (`$ref`); pydantic v2, schemars (2020-12 mode) and zod-to-json-schema all collect shared types under `$defs` at the document root and reference them as `#/$defs/<name>` (this module has no type names, hence the synthetic `rule<N>`). The scan table holds `scan_cap` (1024) distinct rules; rules past it stay inline, and the `max_schema_rules` bound (65536 rules written, then an `x-truncated` stub) applies as for any export. The output of a rule set without sharing is the plain nested form.

**Array roots** (2026-10-11): a root is one `Rule` (`validateJsonRoot` / `validateJsonRootStreaming`) or a
`[]const T` / `[N]T` typed body (`rootRuleFor`); the walker's root rule is generalized from the implicit
object rule, so an array root costs the same one pass, paths render `[i].field`, the structural `Limits` run
first/along as for objects, and `T.validate_rules` is consulted only for a struct `T`.

## Threat model / out of scope
The JSON structural `Limits` are the security-relevant control here (JSON-DoS mitigation on untrusted
bodies); the byte cap (413) bounds size, the structural scan bounds shape. Explicitly out of scope:
`pattern` has no built-in regex engine (a caller's `Pattern.matcher` carries one); `min`/`max` are f64, so a 54+-bit integer BOUND is the nearest double (an integer value is compared with it exactly) (`parseInto` surfaces an
out-of-range decode as a defensive root-level `invalid` error, never a crash); `uuid` format checks
shape only (the version/variant checks are the separate `uuid3/4/5/7` and `uuid_rfc4122` formats). A top-level JSON array is describable (`validateJsonRoot`, `[]const T` bodies: the same `Limits`, errors at `[i].field`). Duplicate JSON object keys are refused at
every depth, known field or not (`json_invalid`, "DuplicateField") — `std.json`'s default, which
the streaming path reproduces by tracking the keys of every open object. Not a security boundary beyond the DoS caps — it does
not authenticate, authorize, or sanitize for injection (SQL/HTML); callers still own that.

**Known limits, recorded and not planned:** typed float fields accept inf/NaN (`1e400` becomes +inf, a query `nan`) unless a bound is set, as pydantic's default; error paths are dotted, so a field named `a.b` reads as nested; `Pattern.matcher` is documented as whole-string while its exported `pattern` is a search; the default `max_total_nodes` (1M) exceeds what the 1 MiB body cap can hold.


## Verification
Run: `scripts/modtest validate` (`zig build test-validate`). Tests: every rule's code+path, cross-field aggregation, nested paths (`a.b`/`a[i]`), malformed/
empty/truncated JSON → clean `json_invalid` (never a panic), structural-limit rejections at each
bound, typed `parseInto` (derived bounds/enums/defaults/optionals, `validate_rules` merge, JSON-type-
error → pathed-error mapping), query coercion/percent-decoding/duplicate-key handling,
`router.Params` validation, byte-golden 400 error-body JSON; middleware tests over the socket-free
`http.Server.serveStream` (golden 400 + handler-not-invoked proof, valid POST → handler sees parsed
body, typed getter, 413 body cap, stacked Query+Body slot chain); an in-process `router`+`http.Server`
+`http.Client` loopback integration run (invalid POST → 400 with handler never invoked; valid POST →
decoded struct; bad query param → 400).

- **Both paths:** cross-field rules are pinned on the tree and the streaming path by `expectBoth` (the same errors from `validateJson` and `validateJsonStreaming`), array roots by `expectRootBoth` (typed `[]const BatchRow` through `expectTypedAgrees`), and each format by a truth table citing the baked-in it follows (`format truth table: ...`).
- **Oracles:** the rule semantics and the JSON Schema export against python-jsonschema and ajv (`schema_oracle_test.zig`, `tools/schema_oracle.py`); go-playground's own verdicts on formats (`go_format_test.zig`, `tools/format_oracle.py`), rules (`go_rule_test.zig`, `tools/rule_oracle.py`) and cross-field ops (`go_cross_test.zig`, `tools/cross_oracle.py`); the query path against Python, Go and WHATWG decoders and pydantic (`query_oracle_test.zig`, `tools/query_oracle.py`); the official JSON-Schema-Test-Suite `format` files (`json_schema_format_test.zig`). Details and producers: Anchoring and `tools/README.md`.
- **Fuzz:** `VALIDATE_FUZZ=<runs>[,<first seed>]` (testkit's deterministic driver, run in the ordinary test binary; harness bodies in `src/root.zig`, labels in `src/fuzz_test.zig`): `json`, `streaming` (tree == streaming), `format`, `cross` (cross-field rules and array roots, tree == streaming), `unique` (against a quadratic model), `compiled` (the compiled typed path gives the walker's errors in the same order), `rules` (the rule vocabulary, tree == streaming == compiled).
- **Cost pin:** `firstDuplicate`'s comparison count is pinned by a test-only counter (`duplicate_comparisons`), which catches a weakened hash that a correct-answer test cannot see.
- **Constant time:** n/a — input validation, no secret.
- **Audit:** the card's `**Audit:**` line is the current score, cumulative over the last whole-module mutation run and the delta runs after it.
- **Bench:** `zig build bench-validate` (`tools/bench.zig`, `tools/go_bench`, `tools/rust_fast_bench`), see Performance.

## Performance

`zig build bench-validate` (ReleaseFast, needs go; `tools/bench.zig` against go-playground/validator, `tools/rust_fast_bench` against garde and Keats/validator): `parseIntoLeaky` bytes in, validated struct out, on four body shapes, each against a decode-only twin so the figure is the net cost of validation. The figures are the card's Performance line, which is authoritative.

## What is deliberately not done

- **No regex engine of its own.** `Pattern.matcher` takes the caller's matcher (any `fn (ctx, string) bool`) together with the expression's source text, which this module never interprets: it is what the exported schema's `pattern` says and what the error message quotes (user decision). The repo's `regex` module could be the default one, see Backlog.
- **Formats left out on purpose:** `file dir image mimetype uds_exists filepath dirpath unix_addr`: "a validator of untrusted input does no filesystem or name-resolution I/O, and path syntax is platform-defined". `mongodb mongodb_connection_string spicedb`: "one vendor's identifiers, a `Pattern.matcher` covers them". The `*_addr` formats check a literal IP (plus port) and refuse a host name, where go-playground resolves it.
- **Where go-playground's format verdicts are not copied, on purpose** (classes in `tools/format_oracle.py`): `cve` rules beyond the CVE schema, the `rgba` alpha dot, bech32-only and unchecked padding in `btc_addr_bech32`, `btc_addr` without a version check, ULID Unicode folding and overflow, `datauri` reading anything after the comma as base64, a hyphen ending an `fqdn` label, `+80` in `hostname_port`, and its panic in `isIP6Addr` on `]:80`. Six more are go breaking the RFC its tag names (the card's Ahead line).
- **Where go differs and this does not follow, each because JSON or Zig has no such thing:** `oneof`/`noneof` on an int compare go's decimal text, here by value, so the entry `"1e1"` matches 10. `omitempty` is positional in go (tags before it still run), here it skips the whole rule. `omitzero` on a struct is "all fields zero" in go, here only `{}`. A pointer to zero has a value in go, and JSON has no pointers: `0` is empty. `containsrune=ab` reads only the first rune in go, here `.contains` is the whole text. `EqualFold` reads every invalid byte as U+FFFD in go, so `\xff` equals `\xfe`; here not, and no JSON or query value reaches that.
- **Left out, with the reason:** `FieldError.Value` and Rust's `params["value"]`, see `Error.param`'s doc. Parameters are on `Error`, not on the wire, because `{path,code,message}` is byte-pinned and consumers parse it. `gt`/`lt` on a string length (go's overload): `min_len`/`max_len` say it, and the JSON Schema form is the same.

## Open

- **`ssn` and `rgb`/`hsl` left as in go, unverified against a primary source.** `ssn` takes area numbers 000, 666 and 9xx; `rgb` and `hsl` take percentages over 100, which CSS clips rather than refuses.

## Backlog / deferred

- **Aggregation memory per error.** `parseIntoLeaky` over a fixed buffer spends about 415 B per kept error plus ~630 B fixed for a 7-byte path and a 30-byte message (measured by a web-server consumer: 4 errors → 2288 B, 8 → 3950 B); a consumer that budgeted 512 B per error for building *and* writing the problem got `"errors":[]` in a 4 KiB scratch and now keeps 1024 B back. Likely the arena-backed `ArrayList` growth (old capacity never reclaimed) plus per-error path/message strings. Ideal: a documented per-error bound, or a `Limits` knob that sizes the error list up front. LOW (no defect; consumers that size scratch by error count are the ones affected).
- **Format wave 1, left for the next wave:** `iso3166_2` (generate the table from `country_codes.go` like the others, ~1,000 entries), `postcode_iso3166_alpha2` and `postcode_iso3166_alpha2_field` (go's per-country regex table; needs a regex per country, the `regex` module could carry it), `timezone` (IANA names; the `tz` module).
- **Recorded LOW findings of the no-panic sweep, not planned:** numeric `one_of` re-parses the allow-list per value; `key_set.clearRetainingCapacity` is O(capacity) per object above the default limits; a caller-raised `Limits.max_depth` lets the tree path recurse that deep; per-element and per-field path strings on valid documents (bounded by `max_total_nodes`); the `enum` message joins the allow-list per error (at most `max_errors`); query rules scan the query once per rule.
- **`date_time`/`time` accept an offset-less value but export `"format":"date-time"`** (review M4), which RFC 3339 and ajv/python-jsonschema refuse (the suite case "no time offset" is skipped), and a leap second at any time of day: the exported schema is stricter than what is enforced. The laxer profile is documented (README). Options: RFC 3339 by default plus an explicit local profile, or export the profile as an `x-` annotation with no `format`. Consumer-visible -- owner's call.
- **Regex-backed `pattern` from the repo's `regex` module.** `Pattern.matcher` is the way in today; adopting `regex` as the default matcher would add a dependency (the engine exists in the repo, its SPEC names this adoption).
- **`parseQueryLeaky`'s `validate_rules` ignores `cross`.** A typed struct has no sibling lookup outside its own fields; follow-up if wanted.
- **Opt-in RFC 9457 answer from the middleware.** The middleware (`Body`/`TypedBody`/`Query`/`PathParams`) answers only in the plain `{"errors":[…]}` shape with `application/json`; answering as problem details (`writeErrorsProblem`, `application/problem+json`) is deferred until a `router`-middleware consumer asks. The one consumer that wanted problem+json calls the core directly, not the middleware.


## Anchoring

**Anchor grade:** class A · oracle EXTERNAL

- **Class A** — wire/interop format — other implementations must byte-agree with it.
- **Oracle EXTERNAL** — published vectors, goldens captured from a foreign implementation, or a test run against a live foreign peer.

**Rule vocabulary.** src/go_rule_test.zig replays go-playground v10.30.5 on 2,525 values over 305 tags (`tools/rule_oracle.py`, frozen; 45 parameterized or combined tags, plus `eq_ignore_case` over 260 cased code points across the planes, which pins the generated fold table to Go's own), on the tree and the streaming path, no difference class needed. src/schema_oracle_vectors.zig gained a second batch from its own seed (37 crafted, 150 generated sets, 1,162 documents), the first batch byte-identical: 504 sets, 3,237 documents, plus the class `IGNORE_CASE`. The `rules` fuzz harness requires tree, walker and compiled path to agree.

**What the tests actually contain.** src/json_schema_format_test.zig runs the official json-schema-org/JSON-Schema-Test-Suite optional/format files (src/testdata/json-schema-test-suite, 12 formats), which is where the isDuration bug was found. src/schema_oracle_test.zig replays python-jsonschema 4.19.2 and ajv 8.20.0 (`tools/schema_oracle.py`, frozen 2026-10-05, re-taken 2026-10-24): 317 rule sets (17 crafted, 300 generated: every kind, `required`, `allow_null`, bounds, code-point and byte lengths, `one_of`, the four built-in patterns, nested `fields`/`items` two deep), each of which must export exactly the frozen schema, and 2075 documents that `validateJson` and `validateJsonStreaming` must answer as both validators do -- or as a named class decides (f64 bounds past 2^53 -- Python decides, since 2026-10-24; `$` before a final newline left with the `(?![\s\S])` export end, `1e400` as an integer, the byte bounds a schema cannot state, an unpaired surrogate escape), each class pinned to at least one case. src/query_oracle_test.zig replays the text path (`tools/query_oracle.py`, frozen 2026-10-06): 39 query strings whose first value of a field must decode as Python's `parse_qsl`, Go's `net/url` and WHATWG `URLSearchParams` decode it, and 336 values against 12 rules (int with no, small, i64 and u64 bounds; float; bool; string lengths, `one_of`, `charset`) that `validateQuery` must accept or refuse with pydantic 2.13.5's error code -- pydantic in lax mode fed the very bytes the module decodes, Go's strconv/math.big and Python's `int()`/`float()` beside it. Six named classes decide where they split (Go drops a pair with a bad escape or a `;`; WHATWG replaces bytes that are not UTF-8; pydantic strips whitespace around a number and takes `5.0` as an int, Go does not and neither does the module; an integer past 2^53 against an f64 bound, compared exactly), each pinned to at least one case. src/go_format_test.zig replays go-playground/validator v10.30.5 itself on its own formats (`tools/format_oracle.py`, `tools/go_formats`, frozen 2026-10-24): 3,289 strings over the 29 formats go has a tag for (crafted edge cases plus seeded mutations), each answered as `validate.Var(s, tag)` does or as a named class decides, every class deciding at least one case. Six classes are go-playground breaking the RFC its tag names (MAPPED_V4, HOSTNAME_253, EMAIL_LOCAL_64, EMAIL_DOMAIN, HTTP_EMPTY_HOST, DT_OFFSET_24 -- the `**Ahead:**` line); the rest are this module's documented profile (EMAIL_QUOTED, EMAIL_NON_ASCII, URL_RFC3986_CHARS, URI_RELATIVE, URI_RFC3986_CHARS, URI_PCT_HOST, UUID_RFC4122_STRICT, CIDR_PREFIX_ZEROS, DT_PROFILE). `lowercase`/`uppercase` match go exactly: their change-sets are generated from Go's `unicode` package (`tools/go_casetables`). Not anchored, and not wire behaviour: the `rulesFor` mapping from Zig types (reflection no foreign implementation has; its bounds are the types' own), `custom`/`matcher` (code), `format` inside the oracles (left to the suite), and the English message text.
